newsitem.title: LITHUANIA: Some key facts on Lithuania as nation votes.
newsitem.headline: Some key facts on Lithuania as nation votes.

text.p: Lithuanians vote on Sunday in the second round of a parliamentary election that is expected to seal the political comeback of independence hero Vytautas Landsbergis in the former Soviet republic. These are some key facts about Lithuania.
POPULATION: 3.7 million (Aug 1996), of which around 81 percent are Lithuanian, 8.5 percent Russian and seven percent Polish with small numbers of ethnic Belarussians, Ukrainians and Jews.
Almost a third of the population lives in rural areas.
LANGUAGES: Official language is Lithuanian. Polish and Russian are also widely spoken.
RELIGION: Close to 80 percent of the population is Roman Catholic.
CAPITAL: Vilnius (population 584,000).
AREA: Total area is 65,200 square kilometers. The southernmost of the former Soviet Baltic republics, it is bordered by Latvia, Belarus, Poland and the Russian Baltic enclave of Kaliningrad.

GOVERNMENT: Lithuania, a democratic republic, has a French-style division of powers between the 141-seat parliament, the cabinet and the president. President Algirdas Brazauskas faces his next election in February 1998.
ECONOMY: Gross domestic product (GDP) is expected to grow by 1.5 percent in 1996 and a bouncy four percent in 1997. It expanded by around three percent in 1995.
Agriculture employs over 20 percent of the country's work force but only accounts for seven percent of GDP.
Annual inflation fell from over 22 percent in September to 18.6 percent in October and may hit 15 percent by the end of 1996.
Unemployment was unchanged at 6.4 percent in October compared with September.

In late summer, Moody's assigned Lithuania a Ba2 rating for its foreign currency debt and a Ba3 for its bank deposits, making it the first former Soviet republic to acquire an international credit rating.

Lithuania initialled an association agreement with the European Union (EU) in June of 1995 and has set its sights on EU membership by 2001. The country is also bidding hard to join the NATO military alliance but most anslysts say it will be left out of the first round of NATO expansion.
MODERN HISTORY: On March 11, 1990, Lithuania's Supreme Council, headed by Vytautas Landsbergis, declared independence from the Soviet Union, which had forcibly annexed the small country in 1940.
An enraged Soviet leadership threw up an economic blockade around the breakaway republic. The pressure forced the government to back down and enter negotiations with Moscow.
Events reached a climax on January 13, 1991, when 13 unarmed Lithuanian civilians were killed while defending the Vilnius TV tower from an attack by an armoured KGB unit.
The following July, seven Lithuanian border guards were murdered at the Medininkai crossing on the border with Belarus.

With the Soviet Union paralysed by the Kremlin coup attempt in August 1991, Lithuania and its Baltic siblings Estonia and Latvia made the final break and declared their independence. It was recognized by Moscow the following month.
Landsbergis and his Sajudis independence movement had a high international reputation, but at home the party was riven with internal strife as it tried to cope with a collapsing economy.

Defying those who had written their political obituary, the former communists, renamed the Lithuanian Democratic Labour Party (LDLP), were swept back into power in the October 1992 parliamentary elections.
The LDLP's comeback was sealed in February 1993 when its leader, Algirdas Brazauskas, won the presidential race.
Brazauskas, who was required by the constitution to suspend his party membership when he became president, will now face a French-style period of co-habitation with the new centre-right parliament.
